stops.name: Mount Tamalpais
stops.addr: Mount Tamalpais State Park, Mill Valley, California
stops.invite: A mountain above the Golden Gate with a name older than California, and once a railway that was called the crookedest in the world.
story: Mount Tamalpais rises north of San Francisco Bay. Wikipedia gives the East Peak as 2,571 feet (784 m) and the West Peak, the highest point, as about 2,560 to 2,579 feet depending on the measurement. The name comes from the Coast Miwok words támal pájiṣ, which the page translates as "west hill". It was first recorded in 1845. The popular "sleeping maiden" legend is described there as having no basis in Coast Miwok tradition.

From 1896 to 1930 the Mount Tamalpais and Muir Woods Railway climbed about 8 miles from downtown Mill Valley to the East Peak on standard-gauge track with geared steam locomotives. It was nicknamed "The Crookedest Railroad in the World". An auto road to the peak was built in the 1920s. California State Parks mentions that volunteers at the Gravity Car Barn share the railway's stories.

Today the mountain is part of Mount Tamalpais State Park. Each summer the Mountain Play Association stages Broadway musicals in the open-air amphitheatre on the slopes, and volunteers staff a fire lookout on the East Peak in summer. The contributor's photo looks out over the bay from the mountain.

facts.t: Wikipedia lists the East Peak at 2,571 feet (784 m); West Peak figures vary between about 2,560 and 2,579 feet.
The name comes from Coast Miwok támal pájiṣ, "west hill", first recorded in 1845.
The Mount Tamalpais and Muir Woods Railway ran about 8 miles from Mill Valley to the East Peak from 1896 to 1930.
The state park is open daily 7:00 a.m. to sunset; East Peak, Pantoll and Bootjack parking areas charge fees.

stops.access: The mountain is a state park open daily from 7:00 a.m. to sunset, and there is no main entrance fee, but the East Peak, Pantoll and Bootjack parking areas charge fees. Check the State Parks page for current hours and road access before you go.

access_check.how: Story read against Wikipedia and the California State Parks Mount Tamalpais page. The park's founding year was not stated on either page, so it is left out. Not walked. Submitted as a test, no old photo shown.

stops.name: Moscone Center
stops.invite: San Francisco's biggest convention hall carries the name of a mayor, and it hosted a first in American politics in 1984.
story: Moscone Center opened in 1981 at 747 Howard Street. The first hall, now called Moscone South, put its main exhibition space underground to keep the building low. Moscone North followed in the early 1990s and Moscone West in 2003. Sources disagree on the North opening year (1991 or 1992).

It is named for George Moscone, who was mayor of San Francisco from January 8, 1976 until November 27, 1978. Before the center was built he had opposed development of the area as a supervisor, then backed a compromise as mayor, and voters approved the measure in November 1976. The Board of Supervisors named the center for him on December 8, 1978.

The center hosted the 1984 Democratic National Convention, which nominated Walter Mondale for president and Geraldine Ferraro for vice president, the first woman nominated for either office by a major party. A multi-year expansion finished around the end of 2018, and the above-ground part of Moscone South was rebuilt.

facts.t: Moscone Center opened in 1981 at 747 Howard Street.
It is named for George Moscone, mayor from January 8, 1976 to November 27, 1978.
The Board of Supervisors named the center a memorial to Moscone on December 8, 1978.
The 1984 Democratic National Convention was held there; Geraldine Ferraro became the first woman nominated for national office by a major party.
Moscone North opened in 1991 or 1992 depending on the source, and Moscone West in 2003.

stops.access: The outside can be seen from the public sidewalks around Howard Street. Entry to the halls depends on the event calendar and is usually by ticket or registration, so check before planning to go in.

access_check.how: Story read against Wikipedia and Exhibit City News. The official Moscone site could not be fetched (robots). Not walked. Submitted as a test, no old photo shown.

stops.sens: The center is named for Mayor George Moscone, who was shot and killed at City Hall on November 27, 1978.
